reasons.A: Most formal and even-paced; long balanced sentences with semicolons and a measured essayist's hush, far from the passage's jaunty, clipped, question-and-fragment movement.
reasons.B: Closest to the passage's chatty first-person irony and abrupt short sentences ('I will make one exception.', 'They are too well off.'), with a dash-led list and a contraction; still smoother than the author's telegraphic fragments.
reasons.C: Some short punchy closers and dry wit, but the diction is genteel and British-leaning and the paragraphs move in steady, well-joined periods rather than the author's staccato asides.
reasons.D: Has a punchy standalone opener and closer and direct 'you' address like the passage's 'riddle' setup, but most sentences are long, even and modern-plain, lacking the author's fragments and quick rhetorical questions.
